prose_changes.old: Benedict of Nursia left Rome for a cave at Subiaco and ended up, around 529, founding a monastery on the hill of Monte Cassino, in an Italy being torn apart first by the Gothic wars and then by the Lombard invasions. What he left behind was a rule. Seventy-three short chapters on prayer, work, sleep, food, guests, discipline and the election of an abbot, much of it adapted from an older and harsher text but shortened, moderated, and written with an eye for what ordinary people could actually sustain. A generation later Gregory the Great, a monk before he was a pope, wrote the only account we have of Benedict's life, and governed the Italian church through a correspondence of more than 850 letters that shows the same world from the other side — famine, plague, refugees, Lombard armies, and the daily management of a church trying to hold itself together.

prose_changes.old: The Rome Gregory was born into around 540 had been besieged, taken, retaken and emptied within living memory. The Gothic wars and Justinian's reconquest had wrecked the city and the countryside that fed it, and from 568 the Lombards held most of the peninsula. The imperial government sat at Ravenna and had little left to spend on Rome. Gregory was city prefect, gave it up, turned the family house on the Caelian into a monastery, and was sent to Constantinople as the pope's representative. He was elected bishop in 590, during a plague, and spent fourteen years doing a job that had quietly become something else. The letters show what it was. He ran the papal estates in Sicily as the city's food supply and audited the men who managed them. He paid soldiers and negotiated with Lombard dukes when the exarch would not. He ransomed prisoners. He told bishops in Gaul, Spain, Africa and Illyricum what he thought they were doing wrong, at length. He refused the title of universal bishop when Constantinople's patriarch used it, and called himself servant of the servants of God instead. And in 596 he sent a party of his own monks to Kent, and then wrote to them again and again about what to do with pagan temples and how far to insist on Roman custom. The Pastoral Rule, written at the beginning of it, is the book underneath all the rest: an argument that the government of souls is the art of arts, that different people must be told the same truth differently, and that wanting the office is itself a disqualification for it.

The Gothic wars and Justinian's reconquest had wrecked the city and the countryside that fed it, and from 568 the Lombards held most of the peninsula. The imperial government sat at Ravenna and had little left to spend on Rome. Gregory was city prefect, gave it up, turned the family house on the Caelian into a monastery, and was sent to Constantinople as the pope's representative. He was elected bishop in 590, during a plague, and spent fourteen years doing a job that had quietly become something else. The letters show what it was. He ran the papal estates in Sicily as the city's food supply and audited the men who managed them. He paid soldiers and negotiated with Lombard dukes when the exarch would not. He ransomed prisoners. He told bishops in Gaul, Spain, Africa and Illyricum what he thought they were doing wrong, at length. He refused the title of universal bishop when Constantinople's patriarch used it. He already called himself servant of the servants of God, a title Pope Damasus and Augustine had used before him. And in 596 he sent a party of his own monks to Kent, and then wrote to them again and again about what to do with pagan temples and how far to insist on Roman custom. The Pastoral Rule, written at the beginning of it, is the book underneath all the rest: an argument that the government of souls is the art of arts, that different people must be told the same truth differently, and that wanting the office is itself a disqualification for it.
prose_changes.reason: 'Called himself servant of the servants of God instead' reads as a reply to the universal-bishop title. It is not: Gregory heads his first letters as pope (Register I.1, 590) with the formula, five years before the dispute of 595, and Barmby's note there says Pope Damasus and Augustine used it before him (npnf212 lines 30976-30987). The rcg world's Doc_02 makes the same correction.

prose_changes.old: The Pastoral Rule became the standard book on the bishop's office in the West: Carolingian councils legislated that bishops should own it and read it, Alfred translated it into English as one of the books he thought most needful for men to know, and it stayed in use for a thousand years. The mission to Kent is why there is an English church in communion with Rome at all, and why anglo-saxon-christianity has a Roman half. And the working model of the bishop of Rome as the practical government of central Italy - feeding the city from church estates, treating with invaders, paying troops - is where the temporal power of the papacy actually begins, whatever later documents claimed for it.
prose_changes.new: The Pastoral Rule became the standard book on the bishop's office in the West. Carolingian councils legislated that bishops should own it and read it. Alfred had it translated into English, meaning, he said, to send a copy to every bishop in his kingdom, and it stayed in use for a thousand years. The mission to Kent is why there is an English church in communion with Rome at all, and why the early English church has a Roman half. And the working model of the bishop of Rome as the practical government of central Italy - feeding the city from church estates, treating with invaders, paying troops - is where the temporal power of the papacy actually begins, whatever later documents claimed for it.
